questions.question: What are the five EC2 pricing models?
questions.answer: On-Demand (pay per second/hour, no commitment), Reserved Instances (up to 72% discount with 1 or 3-year commitment), Spot Instances (up to 90% discount on unused capacity, with interruption risk), Savings Plans (commit to a minimum hourly spend for flexibility), and Dedicated Hosts (entire physical server for compliance and BYOL licensing).

questions.question: What is an On-Demand EC2 instance?
questions.answer: An On-Demand instance is the default EC2 billing model. You pay per second (Linux/macOS) or per hour (Windows) with no upfront payment and no long-term commitment. It is the most flexible but most expensive option, best suited for unpredictable workloads, short-term projects, and development environments.

questions.question: What is a Reserved Instance and how does it differ from On-Demand?
questions.answer: A Reserved Instance is not a different type of server — it is a billing discount applied to an On-Demand instance when you commit to a specific instance type for 1 or 3 years. You get the same EC2 server, but at up to 72% off On-Demand rates. The trade-off is a commitment — if your needs change, you are stuck with the instance type unless you have Convertible RIs or sell on the RI Marketplace.

questions.question: What is the maximum discount available with Spot Instances, and why is it so high?
questions.answer: Spot Instances can be up to 90% cheaper than On-Demand. The discount is high because you are using AWS's unused, idle server capacity. AWS would rather rent it cheaply than leave it empty. The trade-off is that when On-Demand or Reserved customers need that capacity, your Spot Instance receives a 2-minute warning and is terminated.

questions.question: What is the difference between Standard and Convertible Reserved Instances?
questions.answer: Standard RIs offer up to 72% discount but are locked to the original instance family, OS, and region — you cannot change them. Convertible RIs allow you to exchange for a different instance family, OS, or tenancy during the commitment period, but offer a lower discount (up to ~54%). Choose Standard if your workload is stable; choose Convertible if you might need to change instance types.

questions.question: What is the 2-minute warning on Spot Instances?
questions.answer: When AWS needs to reclaim a Spot Instance (because demand has increased and the Spot price has risen above your bid), it provides a 2-minute interruption notice before terminating the instance. This warning is delivered via instance metadata (at the /spot/termination-time endpoint) and via Amazon EventBridge events. Your application should use this time to save state, finish current tasks, or drain connections gracefully.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Dedicated Instance and a Dedicated Host?
questions.answer: Both provide hardware isolation from other AWS accounts, but a Dedicated Host goes further: you get an entire physical server, visibility into socket and core counts, and support for Bring Your Own License (BYOL) software. A Dedicated Instance only ensures no other account shares your hardware — you cannot see physical hardware details and cannot use per-socket or per-core BYOL licenses. Dedicated Hosts are more expensive.

questions.question: When would you choose Savings Plans over Reserved Instances?
questions.answer: Choose Savings Plans when you want Reserved Instance-level savings but with more flexibility. Savings Plans commit to a minimum spend per hour rather than a specific instance type. Compute Savings Plans are the most flexible — they apply to EC2 (any family, size, region, OS), Fargate, and Lambda. If your instance mix changes frequently or you use multiple compute services, Savings Plans are better. If your workload is fixed to a specific instance type and region, Standard RIs provide a slightly higher discount.

questions.question: What types of workloads are best suited for Spot Instances?
questions.answer: Spot Instances are best for fault-tolerant, interruption-tolerant workloads: batch data processing, machine learning model training with checkpointing, big data analytics (Hadoop, Spark), video/image rendering, CI/CD build pipelines, and stateless web servers (as part of a mixed fleet). The common factor is that these workloads can either restart from a checkpoint or tolerate the loss of an instance mid-task.

questions.question: What is Zonal vs Regional scope for Reserved Instances?
questions.answer: A Zonal RI applies only to a specific Availability Zone and provides a capacity reservation — AWS guarantees your instance will launch in that AZ even during peak demand. A Regional RI applies the discount to any instance across the entire region regardless of AZ, but does not provide a capacity reservation. Regional RIs offer more flexibility (no need to predict which AZ); Zonal RIs provide the additional safety net of guaranteed capacity.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to explain cloud cost optimisation to a non-technical stakeholder.
questions.answer: (Situation) I was working on a project where the team had been running all EC2 instances as On-Demand for 18 months. The finance team flagged a $40,000/month EC2 bill and asked for a cost reduction plan. (Task) I needed to analyse usage patterns and propose a pricing model migration without disrupting production. (Action) I used AWS Cost Explorer to pull 12 months of usage data, identified 15 instances running 24/7 with consistent usage, and proposed switching them to 1-year Reserved Instances with All Upfront payment. I presented a simple comparison: current cost vs projected cost, with a payback period of 7 months. (Result) Management approved the migration, and within 2 months of purchasing the RIs, the monthly bill dropped by 38% — saving over $15,000/month.

questions.question: Describe a scenario where Spot Instances caused a problem and how you would prevent it.
questions.answer: (Situation) A data engineering team ran nightly ETL jobs on Spot Instances without checkpointing. The jobs took 6 hours. (Task) One night, the Spot price spiked and all instances were terminated at hour 5 — losing all progress. The job had to restart from scratch, causing a 5-hour delay in data availability. (Action) To prevent recurrence, I added checkpointing every 30 minutes using S3 to store intermediate state, set up EventBridge to detect the 2-minute Spot warning and trigger a graceful shutdown that saved the current checkpoint, and switched to Spot Fleet with a diversified allocation strategy across multiple instance types and AZs. (Result) Over the next 3 months there were two interruptions — both recovered from checkpoint within 4 minutes, and the team maintained the 90% cost savings from Spot.

questions.question: How would you design a cost-optimised EC2 fleet for a web application that has predictable daytime traffic and unpredictable spikes?
questions.answer: (Situation) A production web application needs 10 instances during normal hours and spikes to 30 instances unpredictably. (Task) Design the most cost-optimal architecture. (Action) I would use a mixed fleet strategy: 10 Reserved Instances (1-year, All Upfront) for the guaranteed baseline — these run 24/7 and justify the commitment. For the spike capacity up to 20 additional instances, I would use a combination: 5 On-Demand for fast, reliable scaling and up to 15 Spot Instances for burst capacity using a diversified Spot Fleet. The Auto Scaling Group would be configured to fill new capacity with Spot first, falling back to On-Demand. (Result) The baseline cost drops ~44% with RIs. The spike capacity uses Spot at 70–90% discount. Total fleet cost drops roughly 50–60% vs running all 30 instances as On-Demand.

questions.question: A company is migrating from on-premises to AWS. They have Oracle Database licenses tied to 4 physical sockets. How do you plan their EC2 setup?
questions.answer: (Situation) The company owns Oracle DB licenses priced per physical socket — 4 sockets total. Moving to shared EC2 would make socket counting impossible, voiding the license for BYOL. (Task) Set up EC2 so Oracle licenses remain valid. (Action) I would recommend Dedicated Hosts, specifically hosts in the database instance family. I would select host types where the total socket count matches or is covered by their 4-socket license. I would purchase a 3-year Dedicated Host reservation to reduce the hosting cost. I would also document the host IDs and socket configuration for Oracle license compliance audits. (Result) The company can use their existing Oracle licenses (saving $50,000+ in new license costs) while meeting AWS infrastructure requirements.

questions.question: Your team accidentally left 50 development EC2 instances running over a long weekend. How do you prevent this in the future?
questions.answer: (Situation) A team left 50 dev instances running for 72 hours over a holiday weekend — an unnecessary cost of approximately $2,000. (Task) Prevent similar incidents. (Action) I implemented three controls: (1) AWS Instance Scheduler to automatically stop non-production instances at 7 PM and restart them at 8 AM on weekdays; (2) AWS Budgets alert set to 80% of monthly dev budget with an SNS notification to the team lead; (3) a tagging policy enforced by AWS Config that requires 'Environment' and 'Owner' tags on all instances, making it easy to identify and terminate untagged dev resources. (Result) The following month's dev bill dropped 35% from weekend and overnight savings alone.

questions.question: Explain the mixed fleet strategy and why it is more cost-efficient than using a single pricing model.
questions.answer: (Situation) A production workload runs a minimum of 20 instances all the time, grows to 35 during business hours, and spikes to 60 during peak events. (Task) Choose the most cost-efficient pricing model mix. (Action) Mixed fleet strategy: 20 Reserved Instances (stable, justified commitment, 44–72% discount), 15 On-Demand for business hours growth (reliable, no risk), and up to 25 Spot for peak spikes (70–90% discount, fault-tolerant burst). (Result) Compared to running all 60 as On-Demand, the mixed fleet saves approximately 50–65% on total compute costs. Compared to buying 60 Reserved Instances, you avoid wasting 40 reserved slots that sit idle most of the time.

questions.question: A startup asks you: 'Should we use Reserved Instances from day one?' What do you advise?
questions.answer: (Situation) A startup is launching their first production workload on AWS. (Task) Advise whether to start with Reserved Instances. (Action) My advice: start with On-Demand for the first 3–6 months. Until you have real production traffic data, you cannot reliably predict your instance needs. Committing to Reserved Instances before understanding your usage pattern risks over-provisioning (wasting money on unused RIs) or under-provisioning (buying the wrong types). After 3–6 months, analyse your usage in AWS Cost Explorer — it will show exactly which instances are running steadily and recommend which RIs or Savings Plans to buy. (Result) The startup avoids locked-in commitments during an uncertain growth phase, then makes data-driven RI purchases once patterns are established.

questions.question: How does vertical scaling affect EC2 billing differently from horizontal scaling?
questions.answer: (Situation) A team needs to increase capacity on a running application. (Task) Compare billing impact of the two approaches. (Action) Vertical scaling (resizing the instance) changes the billing rate for that single instance immediately upon resize. If you have a Reserved Instance, resizing to a different family requires a Convertible RI — a Standard RI cannot change families. Horizontal scaling (adding instances) creates new billing lines at the existing instance rate. With horizontal scaling, you can mix pricing models — Reserved for baseline, On-Demand or Spot for added instances — which is the more cost-flexible approach. (Result) Horizontal scaling is generally preferred in AWS because it is more fault-tolerant AND more cost-flexible. Vertical scaling is simpler but less economical at scale.

questions.question: A company has $100,000 of unused Reserved Instances because a product was sunset. What are their options?
questions.answer: (Situation) A product shutdown left $100,000 worth of unused Standard Reserved Instances with 14 months remaining. (Task) Recover value from the unused RIs. (Action) Three options: (1) Sell the RIs on the AWS Reserved Instance Marketplace — other AWS customers can purchase them, and the company recovers a portion of the remaining value. Note: only Standard RIs can be sold, not Convertible. (2) Use the RIs for other workloads in the same region — any qualifying instance type and OS automatically receives the discount. (3) If the RIs were Convertible, exchange them for a different instance family needed by another team. (Result) The RI Marketplace is typically the best option for truly unused capacity, recovering 60–80 cents on the dollar depending on remaining term and instance type demand.

questions.question: You are asked to reduce the AWS EC2 bill by 40% without changing the application architecture. Walk through your approach.
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 bill is $50,000/month, all On-Demand. Goal: reduce by $20,000/month without architecture changes. (Task) Identify and implement cost optimisations. (Action) Step 1 — Analyse with Cost Explorer: identify which instances have been running steadily for 3+ months (candidates for Reserved Instances or Savings Plans). Step 2 — Right-size: use AWS Compute Optimizer to check if any instances are over-provisioned. Downsizing from m5.xlarge to m5.large, for example, halves the On-Demand cost. Step 3 — Purchase Savings Plans or RIs: for steady-state instances, purchase 1-year All Upfront Compute Savings Plans for ~49% discount. Step 4 — Schedule dev/test: stop non-production instances nights and weekends. Step 5 — Spot where possible: migrate batch jobs to Spot. (Result) Typical outcome: right-sizing saves 15–20%, Savings Plans/RIs save 40–72% on committed instances, scheduling saves 40% on dev. Combined, a 40% overall reduction is achievable.

questions.question: Design an EC2 pricing strategy for a global e-commerce platform that runs in 4 AWS regions and expects 3–5x traffic spikes during Black Friday.
questions.answer: The strategy would have three tiers across all four regions. Tier 1 — Stable baseline: purchase 1-year Compute Savings Plans at the average daily load level. Compute SPs apply across all regions automatically, providing ~49% discount on the predictable baseline. Tier 2 — Predictable growth: reserve On-Demand capacity reservations (free reservations, no discount) in specific AZs one week before Black Friday to guarantee instance availability. Launch On-Demand instances for the known scale-up. Tier 3 — Burst: configure Auto Scaling with a Spot Fleet (diversified across instance types and AZs) for the unpredictable peak beyond the baseline. Pre-configure checkpointing on stateless web tier instances. Post Black Friday: release capacity reservations, let Auto Scaling drain Spot Fleet. Result: 40–50% savings on year-round costs; capacity guarantee during peak; Spot used only on the fault-tolerant web tier, never on databases.

questions.question: A startup is growing from 10 to 500 EC2 instances over 12 months. How should their pricing strategy evolve?
questions.answer: Month 1–3 (10–50 instances): Use On-Demand exclusively. Too early to commit — usage patterns unknown, architecture still evolving. Month 3–6 (50–150 instances): Analyse Cost Explorer. Identify 30–40 instances running steadily 24/7. Purchase Compute Savings Plans at that baseline spend level. Apply to EC2, Fargate, Lambda simultaneously. Month 6–9 (150–300 instances): As workloads stabilise, add Standard RIs for the most consistent, high-cost instance families (e.g., m5.2xlarge production web servers). Use Spot Fleet for batch and ML workloads. Month 9–12 (300–500 instances): Full mixed fleet strategy. Governance: enforce tagging (Environment, Team, Product) to enable showback/chargeback. Set up AWS Budgets per team. Use Cost Explorer monthly to identify new reservation opportunities. At scale, the company should target 40–60% of compute on RIs/Savings Plans, 20–30% On-Demand, and 10–20% Spot. This typically reduces the EC2 bill 45–55% vs all-On-Demand.

questions.question: What are the risks of committing to Reserved Instances too early, and how do you mitigate them?
questions.answer: The main risks are: (1) Over-commitment — buying RIs for capacity you don't end up needing (e.g., a product is shut down, architecture migrates to containers). Mitigation: use Compute Savings Plans instead of RIs for new or uncertain workloads — they are more flexible. (2) Wrong instance type — buying m5.xlarge RIs when the architecture migrates to Graviton m6g. Mitigation: prefer Convertible RIs for workloads that may change instance families. (3) Wrong region — buying RIs in us-east-1 when the workload moves to eu-west-1. Mitigation: use Compute Savings Plans (region-independent) or Zonal RIs only for very stable, proven workloads. (4) Lock-in at a higher rate — buying No Upfront at a lower discount then finding All Upfront was available. Mitigation: run pricing model analysis through Cost Explorer before purchasing, and buy All Upfront when cash flow allows. Overall, the safest approach is to commit only to what historical data confirms, and use Savings Plans for ambiguous cases.

questions.question: How would you explain the AWS shared responsibility model in the context of Dedicated Hosts and compliance?
questions.answer: In the AWS shared responsibility model, AWS is responsible for the security OF the cloud (physical hardware, network, hypervisor), while customers are responsible for security IN the cloud (OS, applications, data). With Dedicated Hosts, the boundary shifts slightly in the customer's favour: AWS still manages the physical data centre and networking, but the customer has an additional guarantee that no other customer's workloads have ever run on their allocated physical host. This is important for compliance frameworks like PCI-DSS, HIPAA, and FedRAMP that require evidence of hardware tenancy isolation. The customer can reference their Dedicated Host IDs in compliance audit documentation to prove isolation. However, the customer remains responsible for the OS, application, and data security on the Dedicated Host — physical isolation does not mean the workload is automatically secure.

questions.question: When would you recommend a customer NOT buy Reserved Instances, even if they are running workloads 24/7?
questions.answer: There are several scenarios where Reserved Instances are the wrong choice even for 24/7 workloads: (1) Architecture in flux — if the team is planning a migration to containers (ECS/EKS), serverless (Lambda), or a different instance family within the next 6–12 months, committing to 1-year Standard RIs creates lock-in. Use Compute Savings Plans instead — they apply to Fargate and Lambda as well. (2) Uncertain business future — startups with uncertain revenue or product direction should avoid long-term commitments. Use Savings Plans with a short commitment or stay On-Demand. (3) Data is insufficient — if the workload has been running less than 3 months, there is not enough historical data to make a confident commitment. Wait for Cost Explorer to have 3+ months of data. (4) Low absolute cost — if the instance is small (e.g., t3.micro at $0.0104/hr), the absolute saving from an RI ($46/year) may not justify the time and overhead of managing a reservation. (5) Workload is already Spot-eligible — if the job is fault-tolerant, Spot at 90% discount is far better than RI at 72%.
